authors: Ogrinc, Greg; Davies, Louise; Goodman, Daisy; Batalden, Paul; Davidoff, Frank; Stevens, David
title: SQUIRE 2.0 (Standards for QUality Improvement Reporting Excellence): revised publication guidelines from a detailed consensus process
notes: PMID 26369893; epub 14 Sep 2015. Simultaneously published in other journals (e.g., J Nurs Care Qual 2016;31(1):1-8, doi 10.1097/NCQ.0000000000000153).
about: Describes the development of SQUIRE 2.0 (revision undertaken 2012-2015). SQUIRE 2.0 emphasises the reporting of three key components of improvement work: the use of formal and informal theory, the context in which the work is done, and the study of the intervention(s).

authors: Langley, Gerald J.; Moen, Ronald D.; Nolan, Kevin M.; Nolan, Thomas W.; Norman, Clifford L.; Provost, Lloyd P.
title: The Improvement Guide: A Practical Approach to Enhancing Organizational Performance
notes: ISBN 978-0-470-19241-2 (hardcover, 512 pp. per Wiley-VCH listing). Place: San Francisco. AHRQ PSNet lists a different ISBN (9780470430880), presumably another format. Checked at: https://www.wiley-vch.de/en/areas-interest/finance-economics-law/the-improvement-guide-978-0-470-19241-2
about: Standard text on the Model for Improvement (three questions plus Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles) used for planning and testing changes.

authors: Perla, Rocco J.; Provost, Lloyd P.; Murray, Sandy K.
title: The run chart: a simple analytical tool for learning from variation in healthcare processes
notes: PMID 21228075. Source of the commonly cited run-chart rules (shift, trend, too many/too few runs, astronomical point).
about: Develops a standard approach to the construction, use and interpretation of run charts for healthcare based on the statistical process control literature. Argues that run charts allow teams to understand objectively if changes lead to improvements, with minimal mathematical complexity.

authors: Provost, Lloyd P.; Murray, Sandra K.
title: The Health Care Data Guide: Learning from Data for Improvement
notes: ISBN 978-0-470-90258-5 (paperback). Place: San Francisco. Checked at: https://gov.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-0470902582,descCd-description.html
about: Practical guide to statistical process control for health care improvement, covering run charts, Shewhart (control) charts, Pareto analysis, scatter diagrams, stratification and rational subgrouping.

authors: Benneyan, James C.; Lloyd, Robert C.; Plsek, Paul E.
title: Statistical process control as a tool for research and healthcare improvement
notes: PMID 14645763; PMCID PMC1758030.
about: Overview of statistical process control (SPC) and its primary tool, the control chart, with practical healthcare examples. Notes that SPC combines rigorous time series analysis methods with graphical presentation of data.

authors: Taylor, Michael J.; McNicholas, Chris; Nicolay, Chris; Darzi, Ara; Bell, Derek; Reed, Julie E.
title: Systematic review of the application of the plan-do-study-act method to improve quality in healthcare
notes: PMID 24025320. Co-author first names expanded from initials (UNCONFIRMED).
about: Of 73 included articles, less than 20% (14/73) fully documented the application of a sequence of iterative PDSA cycles, and only 15% (7/47) reported the use of quantitative data at monthly or more frequent intervals to inform progression of cycles.

authors: Ganz, David A.; Huang, Cindy; Saliba, Debra; et al.
title: Preventing Falls in Hospitals: A Toolkit for Improving Quality of Care
publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
notes: AHRQ Publication No. 13-0015-EF; January 2013; Rockville, MD. Prepared by RAND Corporation, Boston University School of Public Health and ECRI Institute (Contract No. HHSA290201000017I TO #1). The ahrq.gov page returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; citation details confirmed via AHRQ PSNet. UNCONFIRMED: first name 'Cindy' for C. Huang.
about: Toolkit focused on overcoming the challenges of developing, implementing and sustaining a hospital fall prevention program, with sections on readiness, managing change, choosing practices, implementation, measuring falls and sustainability.

authors: The Joint Commission
title: Preventing falls and fall-related injuries in health care facilities
notes: Issue 55, September 28, 2015. jointcommission.org returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch; text verified from a PDF copy of the alert hosted by the Wisconsin Hospital Association.
about: States that every year in the United States hundreds of thousands of patients fall in hospitals, with 30-50 percent resulting in injury, and that the average cost for a fall with injury is about $14,000. Reports 465 sentinel-event reports of falls with injuries since 2009, approximately 63 percent of which resulted in death.

authors: Morse, Janice M.; Morse, Robert M.; Tylko, Suzanne J.
title: Development of a scale to identify the fall-prone patient
container: Canadian Journal on Aging / La Revue canadienne du vieillissement
notes: Verified via Crossref metadata (Cambridge University Press); abstract not reviewed.
about: The original development paper for the Morse Fall Scale.

authors: Morse, Janice M.
title: Preventing Patient Falls: Establishing a Fall Intervention Program
notes: ISBN 978-0-8261-0389-5; New York. First edition: Sage, 1997. One retailer lists a 2008 street date. Checked at: https://www.springerpub.com/preventing-patient-falls-9780826103895.html
about: Guide to building and maintaining an institutional fall prevention program, including a clinical section on implementing the Morse Fall Scale and a research section on how the scale works.

authors: Hendrich, Ann L.; Bender, Patricia S.; Nyhuis, Allen
title: Validation of the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model: a large concurrent case/control study of hospitalized patients
notes: PMID 12624858. Erratum in Appl Nurs Res 2003;16(3):208. UNCONFIRMED: first names 'Patricia S.' and 'Allen' expanded from initials, not checked against the article.
about: Case/control study (355 cases, 780 controls) in an acute care tertiary facility assessing more than 600 risk factors; the result is an easy to use validated Hendrich Fall Risk Model with eight assessment parameters for high-risk fall identification.

authors: Aranda-Gallardo, Marta; Morales-Asencio, Jose M.; Canca-Sanchez, Jose C.; et al.
title: Instruments for assessing the risk of falls in acute hospitalized patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis
notes: PMID 23547708. Article number 122. UNCONFIRMED: first names expanded from initials.
about: Meta-analysis of the Morse Fall Scale, STRATIFY and Hendrich II across 14 studies; the STRATIFY tool provided greater diagnostic validity (DOR 7.64). Reassessment showed a significant reduction in the DOR on the MFS, and the authors advise testing instruments before implementation.

authors: Bouldin, Erin L.; Andresen, Elena M.; Dunton, Nancy E.; et al.
title: Falls among adult patients hospitalized in the United States: prevalence and trends
notes: PMID 23143749; NDNQI data July 2006 - September 2008. UNCONFIRMED: first names expanded from initials.
about: Across more than 88 million patient days in 1263 US hospitals, 315,817 falls occurred (rate = 3.56 falls/1000 patient days), of which 26.1% resulted in an injury. Fall rates were highest in medical units and lowest in surgery units.

authors: Oliver, David; Healey, Frances; Haines, Terry P.
title: Preventing falls and fall-related injuries in hospitals
about: Reports whole-hospital rates of between 3 and 5 falls per 1000 bed-days and that between 1% and 3% of hospital falls result in fracture. Concludes the most appropriate approach includes multifactorial interventions with multiprofessional input.

authors: Morello, Renata T.; Barker, Anna L.; Watts, Jennifer J.; et al.
title: The extra resource burden of in-hospital falls: a cost of falls study
notes: PMID 26510807. Costs in Australian dollars. UNCONFIRMED: first names of second/third authors expanded from initials.
about: Patients who had an in-hospital fall had a mean increase in length of stay of 8 days and mean additional hospital costs of $6669 compared with non-fallers. Concludes programs need to target the prevention of all falls, not just the reduction of fall-related injuries.

authors: Currie, Leanne
title: Fall and injury prevention
container: Patient Safety and Quality: An Evidence-Based Handbook for Nurses (ed. Hughes, Ronda G.), Chapter 10
publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
notes: Book chapter; Rockville (MD): AHRQ, April 2008 (Advances in Patient Safety). Free on NCBI Bookshelf. PMID 21328754.
about: Reviews fall and injury prevention across the care continuum, noting that few randomized controlled trials have evaluated fall- and injury-prevention measures in the acute care setting.

authors: Hempel, Susanne; Newberry, Sydne; Wang, Zhen; et al.
title: Hospital fall prevention: a systematic review of implementation, components, adherence, and effectiveness
container: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
notes: PMID 23527904. Companion evidence review to the AHRQ toolkit (RAND). UNCONFIRMED: co-author first names expanded from initials.
about: Fifty-nine studies in US acute care hospitals; most interventions (81%) included multiple components, including care rounds. The pooled postintervention incidence rate ratio was 0.77 (95% CI 0.52-1.12, P = .17; eight studies).

authors: Miake-Lye, Isomi M.; Hempel, Susanne; Ganz, David A.; Shekelle, Paul G.
title: Inpatient fall prevention programs as a patient safety strategy: a systematic review
about: States that multicomponent programs to prevent falls among inpatients reduce relative risk for falls by as much as 30%. Themes associated with successful implementation included leadership support, engagement of front-line staff, a multidisciplinary committee, pilot-testing interventions and staff education.

authors: Cameron, Ian D.; Dyer, Suzanne M.; Panagoda, Claire E.; et al.
title: Interventions for preventing falls in older people in care facilities and hospitals
notes: PMID 30191554; Cochrane review article number CD005465. UNCONFIRMED: co-author first names expanded from initials.
about: Included 95 trials (138,164 participants), 24 in hospitals. In hospitals, multifactorial interventions may reduce rate of falls (RaR 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.01), although subgroup analysis suggests this may apply mostly to a subacute setting.

authors: Dykes, Patricia C.; Carroll, Diane L.; Hurley, Ann; et al.
title: Fall prevention in acute care hospitals: a randomized trial
about: Cluster randomized study in 4 US hospitals of a health-IT fall prevention tool kit (FPTK) built on a nurse-completed fall risk assessment. Site-adjusted fall rates were 4.18 per 1000 patient-days in control units versus 3.15 in intervention units (P = .04); no significant effect was noted in fall-related injuries.

authors: Meade, Christine M.; Bursell, Amy L.; Ketelsen, Lyn
title: Effects of nursing rounds: on patients' call light use, satisfaction, and safety
notes: PMID 16954767. Studer Group study. UNCONFIRMED: first names expanded from initials.
about: Six-week quasi-experimental study on 27 nursing units in 14 hospitals with rounds at one-hour or two-hour intervals. Concludes that a protocol incorporating specific actions into rounds conducted either hourly or once every two hours can reduce call light use, increase satisfaction with nursing care, and reduce falls.

authors: Mitchell, Matthew D.; Lavenberg, Julia G.; Trotta, Rebecca L.; Umscheid, Craig A.
title: Hourly rounding to improve nursing responsiveness: a systematic review
notes: PMID 25148400; PMCID PMC4547690.
about: Systematic review with GRADE analysis. Finds moderate-strength evidence that hourly rounding programs improve patients' perception of nursing responsiveness, and moderate-strength evidence that these programs reduce patient falls and call light use.

authors: Hicks, Deborah
title: Can rounding reduce patient falls in acute care? An integrative literature review
notes: PMID 26306357; no DOI listed in PubMed. UNCONFIRMED: author first name 'Deborah' (PubMed gives only 'Hicks D').
about: Integrative literature review summarising multiple studies that found rounding decreased falls per 1,000 patient days.

authors: Daniels, Joan F.
title: Purposeful and timely nursing rounds: a best practice implementation project
container: JBI Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports
notes: PMID 26878929. Medical-surgical unit, United States. UNCONFIRMED: author first name 'Joan' (PubMed gives only 'Daniels JF').
about: JBI best practice implementation project on a medical-surgical unit; use of a rounding protocol increased to 64% compliance from zero, and patient falls decreased by 50%.

authors: Harris, Ruth; Sims, Sarah; Leamy, Mary; et al.
title: Intentional rounding in hospital wards to improve regular interaction and engagement between nurses and patients: a realist evaluation
notes: PMID 31609565; Southampton (UK), October 2019. UNCONFIRMED: volume 7 issue 35 inferred from DOI hsdr07350; co-author first names expanded from initials.
about: Realist evaluation in English NHS acute trusts; 97% of trusts had implemented intentional rounding in some way, but fidelity to the original Studer Group protocol was generally low. Concludes that the effectiveness of intentional rounding, as currently implemented and adapted in England, is very weak.

authors: Carayon, Pascale; Gurses, Ayse P.
title: Nursing workload and patient safety: a human factors engineering perspective
container: Patient Safety and Quality: An Evidence-Based Handbook for Nurses (ed. Hughes, Ronda G.), Chapter 30
publisher: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
notes: Book chapter; Rockville (MD): AHRQ, April 2008 (Advances in Patient Safety). Free on NCBI Bookshelf. PMID 21328758.
about: Argues that nursing workload is affected by staffing levels and patients' conditions but also by the design of the nurses' work system, and proposes a human factors engineering approach to reduce or mitigate workload.

authors: Aiken, Linda H.; Clarke, Sean P.; Sloane, Douglas M.; Sochalski, Julie; Silber, Jeffrey H.
title: Hospital nurse staffing and patient mortality, nurse burnout, and job dissatisfaction
about: Each additional patient per nurse was associated with a 7% increase in the likelihood of dying within 30 days of admission, a 23% increase in the odds of burnout and a 15% increase in the odds of job dissatisfaction.

authors: Kotter, John P.
title: Leading Change
notes: Boston, MA; 187 pp.; ISBN 978-0-87584-747-4. Checked at: https://archive.org/details/leadingchange0000kott
about: Sets out an eight-stage process for leading organizational change, from establishing a sense of urgency and forming a guiding coalition to anchoring new approaches in the culture.
